script.opening_words:
It's 10:00 p.m. and you're scrolling
Instagram looking at a coworker's baby
announcement. Cute kid, tiny socks, two
parents who already look like they
haven't slept in 6 weeks. And somewhere
in the back of your brain, a little
voice starts doing math you didn't ask
it to do. Diapers, daycare, hospital
bill, the car seat your friend just
complained about costs more than her
first car. You quietly close the app.
You and your partner have been talki
script.ending_words:
he nursery. Open the 529 the week
they're born. Claim every credit and
account you can find. It won't be
enough, but it'll matter. And if the
math doesn't work, then please, for the
love of God, do not let anyone shame you
into doing it anyway. There is no trophy
for having a child you can't afford to
raise without imploding. The smartest
financial decision a lot of Americans
are making right now is the one nobody
on Instagram is posting about. The
decision to wait. The decision to have
one instead of three. The math is
screaming. Most people aren't listening.
You don't have to be most people.
script.analysis: All 19,580 stored characters read in two contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Hook: late-night baby-announcement math. Figures: LendingTree 2026 $303,418 to 18 (+28% from 2023) or ~$414K adjusted; median household income $83,730; Peterson-KFF birth costs ($20,416 gross, $2,743 out of pocket; C-section ~$29K; uninsured), NICU costs, 2026 out-of-pocket maximum; FMLA unpaid leave, 27% private paid family leave access, OECD 18.5 weeks, ~$14,400 lost wages; BabyCenter $20,384 first year; Child Care Aware $13,128 average and metro costs; care.com 20% of income vs HHS 7%; Jack and Emily Denver budget ($156K, $9,400 take-home, $7,600 fixed, $200 saved); mid-video community CTA; motherhood penalty and PNAS child penalty, two-income trap; KFF premiums; housing upgrades; college projections and 529 contributions; $400-500K metro floor and income thresholds; NYC CCC estimate; fertility rate record low; Pew and BYU survey shifts; 2025-2026 policy changes (CTC $2,200, dependent-care FSA $7,500, $1,000 Trump account); France/Denmark/OECD comparisons; close granting permission to wait. Dense, well-researched, emotionally resonant, with a few incorrect numbers. ASR not audio-verified.

claim_audit: 0:9800 LendingTree $303,418 is ~28% above its 2023 $237,482 figure (ratio 1.278) - internally consistent; $303K-$414K over 18 years = ~$17K-$23K/year correct. Median household income $83,730 (Census 2024) correct; $303K-$414K equals ~20-27% of 18 years of median gross income. Peterson-KFF birth cost and out-of-pocket figures, ~1 in 3 C-sections, FMLA 12 unpaid weeks at 50+ employee firms, ~27% private-sector paid family leave access (BLS) and ~$14,400 for 12 weeks of median full-time earnings are consistent. The 2026 ACA family out-of-pocket maximum is ~$21,200; $10,600 is the self-only limit. NICU share/cost figures unverified. Child Care Aware 2024 average $13,128 consistent; Jack and Emily line items sum to $7,600, leaving $1,800 - correct.

9800:19580 KFF 2025 family premium ~$26,993 and worker share ~$6,850 consistent (stored "$26,900 93" garbled). College: four years at ~$62,000 in-state = ~$248,000, but $300/month into a 529 for 18 years grows to only ~$116K (6%) to ~$129K (7%), so it does not "fully fund" the degree; $700/month (~$300K at 7%) likewise falls well short of the stated $575K private cost. General fertility rate ~53.1 per 1,000 as a record low consistent with provisional CDC data; Pew 36% citing cost consistent. 2025 child tax credit $2,200 and 2026 dependent-care FSA $7,500 consistent with 2025 legislation; "first change since 1986" omits the temporary 2021 increase. $1,000 at ~7.7% for 18 years = ~$3,800 correct. US vs OECD per-child childcare spending ($500 vs $14,000) unverified.
